title: The Wolf and the Shepherd
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Wolf hung about near a flock of sheep for a long time, but made no attempt to molest them. The Shepherd at first kept a sharp eye on him, for he naturally thought he meant mischief: but as time went by and the Wolf showed no inclination to meddle with the flock, he began to look upon him more as a protector than as an enemy.

And when one day some errand took him to the city, he felt no uneasiness at leaving the Wolf with the sheep. But as soon as his back was turned the Wolf attacked them and killed the greater number. When the Shepherd returned and saw the havoc he had wrought, he cried, "It serves me right for trusting my flock to a Wolf."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Wolf do near the flock of sheep at first?
options: He circles the flock every night howling loudly
He kills a few sheep right away
He hangs about for a long time without attempting to molest them
He tries to lead the sheep away from the Shepherd

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Shepherd behave toward the Wolf at first?
options: He keeps a sharp eye on him, thinking he means mischief
He welcomes him warmly as a new companion
He ignores him completely from the very start
He drives him away with a stick

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Shepherd's view of the Wolf change over time?
options: He begins to fear him even more than before
He decides to sell the flock and leave the area
He starts training the Wolf to herd the sheep
He begins to see him more as a protector than an enemy

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why does the Shepherd leave the flock alone with the Wolf?
options: He wants to test the Wolf's loyalty
Some errand takes him to the city
He falls ill and cannot tend the sheep
He is called away by another shepherd

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Wolf do as soon as the Shepherd's back is turned?
options: He runs away from the flock entirely
He guards the flock even more closely
He attacks the sheep and kills the greater number
He waits patiently for the Shepherd's return

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Shepherd say when he returns and sees the damage?
options: "It serves me right for trusting my flock to a Wolf."
"I should have never left the city."
"The Wolf must have been provoked by something."
"I will find a new flock tomorrow."

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Shepherd's caution fade away over time?
options: The Shepherd forgets that wolves are naturally dangerous
The Wolf explicitly promises never to harm the sheep
The Shepherd is told by others that the Wolf is harmless
The Wolf's long period of good behavior convinces him the danger has passed

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Wolf's patient waiting suggest about his true intentions all along?
options: He genuinely intended to protect the flock forever
He was waiting for an opportunity when no one could stop him
He was testing whether the sheep trusted him first
He had no interest in the sheep until the Shepherd left

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "molest" mean in "made no attempt to molest them"?
options: To count or track
To feed or nourish
To harm or bother
To herd or guide

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: A period of good behavior does not guarantee that a natural danger has truly disappeared
Wolves can be trained to protect sheep if given enough time
Shepherds should never leave their flocks unattended for any reason
Trusting others always leads to betrayal in the end

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Shepherd originally think the Wolf meant by staying near the flock?
options: Friendship
Curiosity
Hunger for grass
Mischief

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where does the Shepherd's errand take him?
options: To a neighboring farm
To the city
To a nearby market
To visit his family

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Shepherd feel about leaving the flock with the Wolf?
options: He feels great anxiety
He feels regret before even leaving
He feels no uneasiness
He feels confident only for the first hour

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Shepherd blame himself rather than only the Wolf when he returns?
options: He recognizes that he was the one who chose to trust a natural predator
He believes the Wolf could not have known any better
He believes another shepherd is actually responsible
He blames himself for choosing to raise sheep at all

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the timing of the Wolf's attack reveal about his behavior the whole time?
options: His attack was a sudden, uncharacteristic loss of control
His attack happened before the Shepherd actually left
His attack was provoked by the sheep themselves
His earlier calm was patience, not a genuine change in nature

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "havoc" mean in "saw the havoc he had wrought"?
options: A pleasant surprise
Widespread destruction or damage
A minor inconvenience
A carefully planned arrangement

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Wolf protects a flock of sheep for many years without incident
A Shepherd trains a Wolf to guard his sheep successfully
A Shepherd's growing trust in a Wolf is betrayed the moment he leaves the flock unguarded
A Wolf and a Shepherd become lifelong friends
